Here is the student’s answer for this case:
1. Case 1: Left hemimegalencephaly
This 11-year-old boy has refractory right-sided complex partial seizures since infancy, developmental delay, and right hemiparesis, all pointing to a left hemispheric structural focus. MRI shows diffuse left cerebral gyral thickening with FLAIR subcortical U-fiber hyperintensities, midline shift, and left inner-table scalloping, while myelination is normal and there is no contrast enhancement—findings that exclude neoplastic or inflammatory disease and indicate a malformation of cortical development. The radiologist explicitly interprets this diffuse hemispheric pattern as characteristic of hemimegalencephaly, refining the broader hypothesis of left cerebral cortical malformation (0.90) to hemimegalencephaly (0.92). The diffuse hemispheric involvement with midline shift and inner-table scalloping also argues against focal cortical dysplasia (0.05) and polymicrogyria (0.03), while the normal delivery, absent family history, and lack of consanguinity argue against genetic/developmental epilepsy (0.05) and perinatal injury (0.02). Although video-EEG was empty, imaging alone is sufficient to establish the diagnosis. Thus the epilepsy is structural focal epilepsy caused by left hemimegalencephaly.
